paragraphs.text: Parcelbird Now: should we launch our own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
Discussion document for the January 2027 decision meeting
All figures come from the board briefing pack or are derived from it; the derivations are in the appendix (pages 13–14).

slides.title: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business, which can break even within today's cash if growth holds

paragraphs.text: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business, which can break even within today's cash if growth holds
Orders lose money at every level of performance we have seen.

At the median of the 14 customer sites our software runs, each order loses $2.67 before dark-store costs and $6.17 after them. Combining the best value seen at any site on every input, which no single site has managed, still loses $1.76.
Decisions we ask the board to take
The founders' plan turns positive only by beating our best site on three drivers at once.

It assumes a $45 order (best seen: $42), 3.5 orders per rider-hour (best: 3.0), 1,800 orders a day (best: 1,400) and promotions at 2% of order value (every site: 6%). If order value or rider productivity only reaches the median, orders lose money again.
Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to work the 37-grocer pipeline.
Ask management to package the software for grocers who want fast delivery from their own stores, selling to that trend rather than competing with our pipeline.
Our own test and the market point the same way.

The Columbus pop-up lost about $12.57 per order, falling below the median on every driver, and only 22% of customers were still ordering in month three. Both incumbents lose money on every order; QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.
Agree now what would reopen the question (page 12).
The plan breaks the 12-month runway rule even if it works; the software path does not.

Holding 12 months of runway leaves $7.2M to deploy, and the plan needs $9.5M. Adding $0.8M a year of engineering and sales reaches break-even in months 26–32 if growth holds at 45–60% and other costs stay flat.
Source: Parcelbird board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis.

slides.title: Of the founders' four claims, only market growth holds up, and the plan fails both of the board's constraints

paragraphs.text: Of the founders' four claims, only market growth holds up, and the plan fails both of the board's constraints
“Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year”
US quick-commerce grocery sales rose from $1.8B (2022) to $5.1B (2025), or 41.5% a year compounded.
No operator is named as owning it. But the one regional operator, QuickBasket, loses $3.40 per order and closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025; an open market may simply be an unprofitable one.
“We know how to run them better than anyone”

Our six-week Columbus pop-up was below our customers' median on all four drivers: order value $31 vs $34, promotions 12% vs 6%, 2.1 vs 2.4 orders per rider-hour, 280 vs 900 orders a day. Six weeks is early, but order value and promotions depend little on ramp-up.
Requires order value, rider productivity and store density all above the best of the 14 sites at once, and promotions at one-third of the benchmark (pages 5–7).
Path to profitability within current cash
At benchmark-median performance a mature dark store loses about $2.0M a year, so nine would lose about $18M a year, more than the $12.0M we hold. A new round is “unlikely”.
At least 12 months of runway at all times
The plan needs $9.5M to month 18; only $7.2M is available above a 12-month reserve (page 9).
Source: Parcelbird board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis.

slides.title: The market is growing about 40% a year, yet both incumbent operators lose money on every order

paragraphs.text: The market is growing about 40% a year, yet both incumbent operators lose money on every order
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

Demand is not the question. Growth has not produced profit: the larger operator loses less per order than the regional one, but neither covers its costs. The board's question is whether any operator, including us, can make money on each order.
Source: Parcelbird board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis.

All three profitable cases need both the $45 order and 3.5 orders per rider-hour, and each is above the best site we have seen.

Two of the three target cities are considering minimum pay for delivery workers. Each extra $1 per rider-hour costs $0.29 per order at plan productivity ($0.42 at the median); $7.06 more an hour (+40%) erases the plan's margin on its own.

slides.title: Scaling the software business breaks even within today's cash if growth stays at 45% or more and other costs are held

paragraphs.text: THE ALTERNATIVE: SCALE THE SOFTWARE BUSINESS
Scaling the software business breaks even within today's cash if growth stays at 45% or more and other costs are held
Cash balance by month under three growth rates for software ARR, $M
The pipeline can support the growth
37 grocers in the pipeline, 9 at the late stage, at an average $96,000 a year.
Late-stage deals alone add $0.86M of ARR (+21%); the whole pipeline would add $3.55M (+87%).
Growing 60% in 2027 means about $2.5M of new ARR, roughly 26 contracts at $96,000, net of churn.
Several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which needs the inventory, picking and dispatch tools we already sell.
Cost discipline matters as much as growth

If other costs rise 10% a year, 60% growth still breaks even (month 32, low of $3.1M), but 45% growth runs out of cash. At 30% growth, runway falls below 12 months from month 23 even with costs held flat.

Illustrative Parcelbird model: $12.0M cash and $4.1M ARR in January 2027; revenue = ARR; 81% gross margin; operating costs held at today's implied $8.1M a year (gross profit + $4.8M burn) plus $0.8M for new hires; growth is net of churn. Not a substitute for a bottom-up plan.

slides.title: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, back a software-led plan, and agree in advance what would reopen the question

paragraphs.text: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, back a software-led plan, and agree in advance what would reopen the question
Reopen the operator question only if all three hold
Decline Parcelbird Now for 2027. No dark stores, no capex.
Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires.
Adopt a runway floor of 12 months, reported at every board meeting against a monthly plan.
Mandate a fast-delivery-from-store offer for pipeline grocers.
Put the new sales hires on the 9 late-stage grocers ($0.86M of ARR).
Scope the store-based offer with 3–5 pipeline grocers who want fast delivery.
Finance to replace page 11 with a bottom-up operating plan, with cost growth explicit.
Close the pop-up and confirm how month-three retention was measured.
A dark store in our customer network covers its own costs (positive after store costs) for two consecutive quarters. Today even the best combined inputs give −$1.76 per order.
Rider minimum-pay rules in the target cities are settled, and the economics re-tested at the new rate.
Software is at break-even, so any venture can be funded without touching the 12-month reserve.

A possible first-mover position in Midwest quick commerce. With QuickBasket retreating and Zipcart still losing $1.90 per order at $1.2B of revenue, we judge that position to be worth less than the cash and focus it would cost.
Source: Parcelbird board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis.

slides.title: How we handled gaps in the briefing pack, and what management should confirm

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX B: METHOD AND OPEN QUESTIONS
How we handled gaps in the briefing pack, and what management should confirm

Two contribution measures. “Before store costs” covers every per-order cost; “after store costs” also spreads each dark store's fixed cost over its orders. The pack does not define the founders' or incumbents' “contribution per order”, so we show both.
The $9.5M plan figure. The pack does not say whether it includes today's $0.4M a month burn, so page 9 shows both readings. The conclusion holds under either.
Runway = cash ÷ current monthly burn. We test the reserve at today's burn, the most lenient basis.
Timing. The $12.0M is treated as cash available in January 2027; the pack does not date it.
Software path (page 11) is a top-down illustration with stated assumptions, not a forecast.
Pop-up exit rate of about 410 orders a day assumes steady 18% weekly growth across the six weeks (11,800 orders in total).
Waterfall (page 6) is sequential. A different order changes the step sizes, not the end points.
How was 22% month-three retention measured in a six-week test?
Does the $9.5M include today's software burn, and what ramp from launch to 1,800 orders a day does it assume?
Is there evidence from any operator, beyond our 14 sites, of 1,800 orders a day or 3.5 orders per rider-hour?
Which minimum-pay proposals are under discussion, at what rate, and in which two cities?
Which pipeline grocers would see Parcelbird Now as a competitor, and how much ARR do they represent?
Source: Parcelbird board briefing pack. The pack labels its company, competitor and market figures as synthetic benchmark data. No external research was used.
